title: The Hydraulic Engineer and the Myth of the General Strike: from Cherbourg to the vault at Tenay
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Boy Sent to the Examination

stops.name: Cherbourg, born to a merchant of oils and gaseous waters
stops.date_confidence: attested; birth date and place given by French and English Wikipedia. The father's trade is 'marchand d'huiles et d'eaux gazeuses' in the French article, oils and carbonated waters, not the wine and mineral water reported by one gathering pass.
stops.campa: In the naval port of Cherbourg, on the second of November, a son is born to a merchant dealing in oils and carbonated waters and to a mother the record calls very pious. The house is provincial, Catholic, commercial, and small. His cousin Albert Sorel will become one of the Third Republic's diplomatic historians and sit in the Academy. Georges will spend twenty-three years on harbours, roads and irrigation channels before he publishes a line, and he is forty-two years old when the first one appears.
suggested_refs: The Cherbourg commercial registers of the 1840s, for the trade in oils and eaux gazeuses

stops.name: Paris, boarded at the Collège Rollin on the rue des Postes
stops.date_confidence: year attested (English Wikipedia: he 'moved to Paris in 1864 to attend the Collège Rollin'); month is an inference from the school year. No source says the family moved with him. The coordinate is the school's pre-1876 site on the rue des Postes, today rue Lhomond, per French Wikipedia 'Lycée Jacques-Decour'; the avenue Trudaine building did not yet exist.
stops.campa: At sixteen he is sent alone to Paris and boarded at the Collège Rollin, then standing on the rue des Postes on the flank of the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève. The school exists to feed the entrance examinations of the state technical corps, and the province sends it merchants' sons by the hundred. He works one year at mathematics in a city he does not yet know. The building he sits in will be abandoned twelve years later for a new one on the avenue Trudaine, and the school will not take the name Jacques-Decour until a resistance schoolmaster is shot in 1942.
suggested_refs: The rue Lhomond site of the old Collège Rollin, 5th arrondissement

stops.name: Paris, the École Polytechnique, promotion of 1865
stops.date_confidence: attested as promotion X1865 by French Wikipedia; the month is the school's ordinary entry date, inferred. The coordinate is the school's nineteenth-century campus in the rue Descartes, not the modern Palaiseau site.
stops.campa: He enters the École Polytechnique with the promotion of 1865, into the barracks-school in the rue Descartes: mathematics, mechanics, drawing, and a uniform. The graduates are sorted into the corps that build the country, and Sorel is ranked out into the Ponts et Chaussées, the engineers of roads, bridges and water. No politics of his from these years is recorded anywhere, and he will publish nothing at all for another twenty-four. In 1869, twenty-one years old, he enters the Corps as a state engineer.
suggested_refs: The École Polytechnique matriculation registers, promotion X1865

segments.name: Twenty-Three Years in the Corps des Ponts et Chaussées

stops.name: Corsica, the first posting
stops.date_confidence: only the end of this posting is attested: English Wikipedia gives 'Stationed in Corsica until June 1871'. No consulted source supplies a start year, and none names the Corsican town where he lived; Ajaccio is used as the island's administrative seat for the service. A gathering pass proposed 1870 as the start; that year appears in no source.
stops.campa: His first posting sends him across to Corsica, to roads and hydraulic works on an island where the state's engineering is thin and its distances long. He is there when the Empire falls at Sedan, there through the siege of Paris and the Commune, and he leaves in June 1871 with the Republic three months old and thirty thousand dead in the streets of the capital behind him. What he built on the island, and what he thought of that year, nothing reachable records. He is twenty-three and has published nothing.
suggested_refs: Service records of the Ponts et Chaussées for Corsica, 1869-1871

stops.name: Albi, one of the southern towns
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. English Wikipedia says only that after Corsica he was 'posted to various places in southern France, Albi, Gap, and Draguignan', with no dates and no ordering. The defensible window is 1871-1876, between Corsica and Mostaganem; the date here orders the segment and asserts nothing.
stops.campa: Reassigned to the mainland, the engineer is posted to Albi on the Tarn, under the great brick cathedral, in a department of coal and glass and river traffic. No letters survive from these years and no one who met him then thought to write him down. The work is the ordinary work of the Corps: surveys, roadbeds, weirs, the arithmetic of water. He is passed from town to town as the service requires, one of several hundred men doing the same thing across the south.
suggested_refs: Departmental archives of the Tarn, Ponts et Chaussées series

stops.name: Gap, the Hautes-Alpes station
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; same 1871-1876 window as Albi, with the same absence of source dates or ordering. The date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: At Gap, in the Hautes-Alpes, the work is mountain water: torrents that take a road out in a night, snowmelt, the retaining of what falls too fast. An engineer here learns that a system holds until the moment it does not, and that the moment cannot be read off the ordinary run of days. He is in his middle twenties, unmarried, moved every few years at the service's convenience, and by every account reaching this far a competent official of the Third Republic. Gap in the 1870s is a town of under ten thousand souls with a bishop and a garrison.
suggested_refs: Departmental archives of the Hautes-Alpes, Ponts et Chaussées series

stops.name: Draguignan, the Var
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; same 1871-1876 window, no source dates, no ordering. Placed last of the three southern towns only because Mostaganem follows in 1876.
stops.campa: Draguignan, then the prefecture of the Var, is the third of the southern stations, a town of olive country and red earth under the Provençal Alps. The file of his career reads like a timetable: a town, a service, a transfer, a town. He is nearing thirty. The men who will matter to him are children or unborn. The Confédération générale du travail does not exist and will not for twenty years, and the words myth and general strike have not yet been put together in any language. He draws plans and forwards them upward.
suggested_refs: Departmental archives of the Var, Ponts et Chaussées series

stops.name: Mostaganem, engineering in colonial Algeria
stops.date_confidence: attested as a range by English Wikipedia: 'Between 1876 and 1879 he was in Mostaganem, in colonial Algeria.' Month unknown, defaulted to January.
stops.campa: He crosses to Algeria and spends three years at Mostaganem, a port on the Oran coast forty-six years into the French occupation, where the state's engineering serves settlement: harbour works, water brought to colonial farms, roads laid through a country conquered within living memory. The man who will later write that violence is the honest form of a conflict is here an instrument of that administration, inside a system that preferred to call itself civil works. He leaves no recorded opinion of any of it.
suggested_refs: Archives of the service des ponts et chaussées, département d'Oran, 1876-1879

stops.name: Perpignan, chief engineer of the hydraulic service
stops.date_confidence: the post and its title, 'ingénieur en chef du service hydraulique', are attested by French Wikipedia, held until the 1892 resignation; English Wikipedia has him at Perpignan for 'the last years of his career until his retirement in 1892'. The start is inferred from the close of the Algerian posting in 1879. A gathering pass proposed 1880, a year found in no source, and another dated 'chief engineer' to 1869, which conflicts with the French article.
stops.campa: At Perpignan he takes charge of the hydraulic service of the Pyrénées-Orientales and holds it for thirteen years, the longest and last stretch of his official life: irrigation canals off the Têt, flood works, the distribution of water among growers who have quarrelled over it for centuries. He is now the chief engineer, with subordinates and a signature that matters in the department. He is also, in the evenings, beginning to read philosophy, meteorology, the history of religion, and the Romans.
suggested_refs: Archives départementales des Pyrénées-Orientales, service hydraulique, 1879-1892

stops.name: Perpignan, the first two books at forty-two
stops.date_confidence: attested: both books appear in 1889 and are listed in the standard bibliographies. Month not recorded. This pair is the firm anchor for a vaguer claim in the pool that he 'began publishing in the second half of the 1880s', which no source dates precisely.
stops.campa: The chief engineer publishes two books in one year: Le Procès de Socrate and Contribution à l'étude profane de la Bible. The first argues that Athens was right to be afraid of Socrates, that the philosopher's questioning dissolved the civic virtues a city lives by; the second reads scripture as a historian reads any other document. At forty-two he has declared in print that reason corrodes what holds a people together. Alcan prints the Socrates in Paris, Ghio the Bible study. He is entirely unknown.
suggested_refs: Le Procès de Socrate (Paris, Alcan, 1889)
Contribution à l'étude profane de la Bible (Paris, Ghio, 1889)

stops.name: Perpignan, chevalier of the Légion d'honneur
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia as an award for his engineering service; the exact date and the promotion decree were not located in the sources reachable for this file.
stops.campa: The Republic makes him a chevalier of the Légion d'honneur for his service as an engineer. It is the ordinary crown of an ordinary technical career, arriving twenty-two years in: a decree, a ribbon, a line in a register at the ministry. He accepts it. The following year he walks out of the career that earned it, and the state that pinned it on him never gives him anything again, no chair, no commission, no post, no second honour. He is decorated once, in 1891, for water works in the Pyrénées-Orientales.
suggested_refs: Base Léonore, Légion d'honneur dossier for Georges Sorel

stops.name: Perpignan, the resignation at forty-five
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested by both English and French Wikipedia; the month is not recorded and defaults to January.
stops.campa: At forty-five he resigns the hydraulic service and leaves the Corps des Ponts et Chaussées, with a pension and twenty-three years of state employment behind him. Nobody is dismissed and nothing is scandalous. The pension is an engineer's pension, and it is what he lives on for the rest of his life. He will publish for the next thirty years without ever holding a chair, a party card, a newspaper of his own, or any position whatever. He simply stops building water works and starts reading.
suggested_refs: Retirement dossier, Corps des Ponts et Chaussées, 1892

segments.name: The House at Boulogne and the Second Life

stops.name: Paris, the return of the retired engineer
stops.date_confidence: the move to the Paris region on retirement is attested by English and French Wikipedia; the month is an ordering inference. The coordinate is the standing Paris pin used across this corpus, inherited byte-identical.
stops.campa: He comes back to the capital he left as a student twenty-seven years before, this time with a pension, a library, and no employer. Paris in 1892 is a city of small reviews: a man with an income and an argument can be read within a year by everyone who matters to him, without ever meeting an editor who could pay him. Sorel takes up the reviews. He is not a journalist and not a professor. He holds no post in any institution in the city and applies for none.
suggested_refs: The Paris review culture of the 1890s, milieu of Sorel's entire second career

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, the house with Marie David
stops.date_confidence: attested that he settled at Boulogne-sur-Seine, today Boulogne-Billancourt, with his companion Marie David, whom he never married; French and English Wikipedia report his mother's opposition as the reason. The month is an ordering inference and the street address was not found in any consulted source.
stops.campa: He settles at Boulogne-sur-Seine, on the western edge of Paris, in a modest house with Marie Euphrasie David, a working woman he has lived with for years and never marries. The reason given is his mother's refusal. He will stay in this house for thirty years and die in it. Everything he is remembered for is written here, at a table in a suburb, by a man who is legally a bachelor and in practice a husband. No source reachable gives the street, or the number on the door.
suggested_refs: The house at Boulogne-sur-Seine, address unlocated in the consulted sources

stops.name: Paris, Bergson's lectures at the Collège de France
stops.date_confidence: attendance is attested by both English and French Wikipedia, which name Bergson among his influences and say he followed the lectures at the Collège de France. No source gives the years or the courses; the date orders the segment only. The coordinate is the Collège de France on the place Marcelin-Berthelot.
stops.campa: Free of the provinces, he goes to hear Henri Bergson lecture in the place Marcelin-Berthelot. Bergson is arguing that lived time is not the divisible time of the engineer's tables, that a duration is undergone and cannot be reassembled from instants. Sorel, who has spent twenty-three years computing flows, takes from it the thing that will separate him from every orthodox Marxist in France: a revolution is not a calculation and does not arrive on a schedule. It is undergone or it does not happen.
suggested_refs: Bergson's courses at the Collège de France in the 1890s
Henri Bergson, Essai sur les données immédiates de la conscience (1889)

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, the declaration for Marxism
stops.date_confidence: the year of his public adherence to Marxism and socialism is attested by English and French Wikipedia; the month is an ordering inference and no source names the article or occasion of the declaration.
stops.campa: One year after leaving the state's service, Sorel declares himself publicly for Marxism and socialism. He is forty-six, comes to Karl Marx through books rather than through any party, and will read him for the rest of his life as a moralist of struggle rather than a science of history. He joins no organisation and holds no card. No source names the article, or the occasion, on which the declaration was made. He begins to write in the small Marxist reviews, at length.
suggested_refs: Karl Marx, Capital, in the French readings available to Sorel in the 1890s

stops.name: Paris, L'Ère nouvelle and Le Devenir social
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia that he wrote for France's early Marxist journals L'Ère nouvelle and Le Devenir social and for the anarchist review L'Humanité nouvelle; the pool gives the mid-to-late 1890s as the range and 1894 as an ordering date, not a source date.
stops.campa: He writes for L'Ère nouvelle and Le Devenir social, the first Marxist reviews France has, and for the anarchist L'Humanité nouvelle, which will print anyone with an argument. His subjects wander: Vico, whose cycles of nations he takes seriously when nobody in Paris does, the Church, Roman law, the crafts of the workshop. Vico had written that men make their own history and can therefore know it. Sorel is assembling, out of that and out of Marx, a socialism whose engine is not economics.
suggested_refs: Georges Sorel, Étude sur Vico (Le Devenir social, 1896)
Giambattista Vico, Scienza nuova

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, the death of Marie David
stops.date_confidence: the year of her death is attested by French Wikipedia, as is the later dedication of Réflexions sur la violence to her memory. No source consulted gives the month, the cause, or her age.
stops.campa: Marie David dies in 1897. He is fifty years old. They have lived together for years unmarried, at his family's insistence and against his own habits of loyalty, and she leaves him a widower in fact and nothing at all in law. Eleven years later he will put her name at the front of the book that makes him famous, which is the only public statement he ever makes about her. No source consulted gives her age, her origin, or what she died of. He stays in the house.
suggested_refs: The dedication of Réflexions sur la violence (1908) to the memory of Marie David

stops.name: Paris, taking Bernstein's side against the orthodox
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia that in the 'crisis of Marxism' debate Sorel took the side of Eduard Bernstein's revisionism and passed through a reformist, pro-Dreyfusard phase. The date is approximate, tied to the Bernstein controversy of roughly 1898-1900, and the pool gives no precise anchor.
stops.campa: The German revisionist Eduard Bernstein has said aloud that the predicted collapse of capitalism is not arriving, and European socialism splits over whether to admit it. Sorel takes his side, against the orthodox who answer the awkward facts by ruling them out of the science. He is at the same time a Dreyfusard, arguing for revision of the case and for the officer's innocence. This is the reformist Sorel, and it lasts about five years before he turns on everything he is now defending.
stops.quote: Rather than abandon their theories, they preferred to declare that the most important facts were mere anomalies, which science must ignore if it is to obtain a real understanding of the whole.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Introduction to the First Publication
suggested_refs: Eduard Bernstein, Die Voraussetzungen des Sozialismus (1899)

stops.name: Paris, Le Mouvement socialiste
stops.date_confidence: attested that Sorel was a regular contributor to Hubert Lagardelle's Le Mouvement socialiste, the Paris review of revolutionary syndicalism, across roughly 1899-1914; the month is an ordering inference. The pin is the standing corpus Paris coordinate, not the review's street address, which was not located.
stops.campa: Hubert Lagardelle's Le Mouvement socialiste becomes the place where Sorel is read. It is the theoretical organ of revolutionary syndicalism: the doctrine that the union, not the party and not the parliament, is the body in which the working class exists, and that its weapon is its own refusal to work. Sorel contributes for fifteen years, alongside militants who actually run strikes. He agrees with them about parliament and disagrees with almost everyone about why.
stops.quote: Revolutionary syndicalism keeps alive in the minds of the masses the desire to strike, and only prospers when important strikes, accompanied by violence, take place.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Introduction to the First Publication
suggested_refs: Le Mouvement socialiste, ed. Hubert Lagardelle, Paris 1899-1914

stops.name: Paris, the doctrine the CGT is already practising
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. That Sorel theorised a general-strike and direct-action doctrine already circulating in the CGT is clear; that he drew specifically on Émile Pouget, who had been publishing sabotage and general-strike propaganda since 1896 and edited La Voix du Peuple from the Bourse du Travail, is an inference from shared doctrine, city and decade, not from a citation located in this pool. No source consulted places Sorel at the Bourse du Travail, so this stop stays at the Paris pin.
stops.campa: The theory has a practice that came first. Since the Toulouse congress of 1897 the Confédération générale du travail has carried sabotage and direct action in its doctrine, and Émile Pouget has been printing both, week after week, in language written for men who cannot spare an evening on philosophy. Sorel supplies the argument for why it works, and it is not an economic argument: the strike is how a class comes to know itself as one. On what a strike does to a prefect, he is entirely concrete.
stops.quote: It is becoming more and more evident every day that working-class violence possesses an extraordinary efficacity in strikes: prefects, fearing that they may be obliged to use force against insurrectionary violence, bring pressure to bear on employers in order to compel them to give way.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Chapter 1, 'Class War and Violence'
suggested_refs: Émile Pouget, La Voix du Peuple, organ of the CGT
The CGT congress of Toulouse, September 1897
sources: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. Hulme (1915), Wikisource

stops.name: Paris, Édouard Berth
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date. Berth is attested as Sorel's closest disciple and collaborator, and they appear together in the Cité française and Cercle Proudhon material of 1910-1911; the pool's source for their alliance from about 1900 is 'general secondary literature', which is not a citation, and a claim that Berth was Sorel's biographer is unsupported and is dropped here.
stops.campa: Édouard Berth attaches himself to Sorel and stays attached for the rest of Sorel's life: the disciple who follows every turn, including the turns nobody else follows. He is a polemicist in his own right and will publish Les Méfaits des intellectuels in 1914, a book against the class that lives by talking, written by a man who lives by talking. Around the two of them a small circle forms of syndicalists, ex-Marxists and young men who despise the Republic for reasons they have not yet sorted out.
suggested_refs: Édouard Berth, Les Méfaits des intellectuels (1914)

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, the pages that go to Rome
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia that in 1905 Reflections on Violence began appearing in Il Divenire sociale, the Rome review; the composition is placed at Boulogne, his established residence, by inference, and no source consulted records Sorel travelling to Rome, so the stop stays at his own house. A gathering pass treated the Rome serialization and the later Paris one as a contradiction between sources; they are two different serializations.
stops.campa: The book that will carry his name starts as instalments posted to Italy. From 1905 the chapters appear in Il Divenire sociale, the Rome review of the Italian revolutionary syndicalists, in Italian, before French readers have seen a word of it. Italy will keep this habit of receiving him first, and it will cost him, after his death, the reputation he could not defend. He is fifty-eight, writing at a suburban table for a movement in another country, and no source records him ever setting foot in it.
stops.quote: if we desire to discuss Socialism with any benefit, we must first of all investigate the functions of violence in actual social conditions.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Introduction to the First Publication
suggested_refs: Il Divenire sociale, Rome, serialization of 1905

stops.name: Paris, the French serialization in Le Mouvement socialiste
stops.date_confidence: the French serialization in Le Mouvement socialiste in 1906 is attested by French Wikipedia; the month is not recorded. This is a separate serialization from the Italian one begun in 1905, not a competing date for the same event.
stops.campa: In 1906 the text appears in French, in Lagardelle's review, where the militants who might act on it can read it. Its centre is a distinction almost nobody wants: between the force that keeps an order standing, exercised by states, police and employers, and the violence of a class that means to end that order. Sorel is not calling for slaughter. He is saying that a movement that will not fight has already agreed to be governed, and that its leaders will end as ministers.
stops.quote: The myth must be judged as a means of acting on the present; any attempt to discuss how far it can be taken literally as future history is devoid of sense.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Chapter 4, 'The Proletarian Strike'
suggested_refs: Le Mouvement socialiste, Paris, serialization of 1906

stops.name: Paris, Réflexions sur la violence in book form
stops.date_confidence: the 1908 book publication in Paris is attested by English and French Wikipedia; the month is not recorded. One gathering pass placed this publication at Perpignan, a city Sorel left permanently in 1892; the error is not carried forward.
stops.campa: Collected between covers in Paris, dedicated to the memory of Marie David, the book makes its argument in one move. The general strike is not a plan and not a forecast. It is a myth: an image of the final day, held whole and undivided, which gives every ordinary strike its meaning and every striker the sense of standing in a war rather than in a negotiation. Whether the day ever arrives is beside the point, and asking is a category mistake. What the image does, it does now, to the men who hold it.
stops.quote: the anticipations of the future take the form of those myths, which enclose with them all the strongest inclinations of a people, of a party or of a class
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Chapter 4, 'The Proletarian Strike'
suggested_refs: Réflexions sur la violence (Paris, Pages libres, 1908)

stops.name: Paris, Les Illusions du progrès
stops.date_confidence: attested by English and French Wikipedia that Les Illusions du progrès appeared in the same year as Réflexions sur la violence; the month is an ordering inference, and the order of the two books within 1908 is not established by the sources consulted.
stops.campa: The same year he publishes the other half of the case. Progress, in Les Illusions du progrès, is not a fact about history but a doctrine invented by a rising bourgeoisie to explain why it deserved to rise, and inherited by a socialism that now expects the future to arrive on its own. The engineer who spent twenty-three years computing what water would do is arguing that history has no such tables. Optimism, he writes, is the enemy: it makes men wait.
stops.quote: Socialism is a philosophy of the history of contemporary institutions
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Introduction to the First Publication
suggested_refs: Les Illusions du progrès (Paris, 1908)

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, the Italian correspondents
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. English Wikipedia supports a phase in which Sorel explored a synthesis of syndicalism and nationalism and was in contact with Italian syndicalists; the 1906-1909 bounds appear in no consulted source and the date here orders the segment, falling inside that window without asserting it. No source records him travelling to Italy, so the stop is at his own house.
stops.campa: Italy answers before France does. The Italian revolutionary syndicalists have been printing him since 1905, and among them are men who will spend the next fifteen years trying to weld the workers' refusal to the nation's honour. Sorel corresponds, argues, and explores the same welding himself. In 1901, at a normal school in Forlimpopoli, a nineteen-year-old boarder named Benito Mussolini had already been reading him alongside Nietzsche and Blanqui.
stops.quote: Strikes have engendered in the proletariat the noblest, deepest, and most moving sentiments that they possess; the general strike groups them all in a co-ordinated picture
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Chapter 4, 'The Proletarian Strike'
suggested_refs: Il Divenire sociale and the Italian syndicalist reviews, 1905-1909

stops.name: Paris, in the orbit of Action française
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia as a marginal and brief involvement with Charles Maurras's royalist circle, given a range of 1909-1910. Historians disagree about how deep it went and this file does not adjudicate that.
stops.campa: Disgusted with a parliamentary socialism he thinks has turned into a career ladder, Sorel drifts toward the royalists of Charles Maurras, who hate the Republic for opposite reasons and are glad to have him. The involvement is marginal and it is short. What the two sides share is contempt for the deputy, the professor and the optimist. What they do not share is anything whatever about who should rule, and Sorel never once writes that a king should. How far the drift went is still argued by historians who read the same pages and come away with different men.
stops.quote: A social policy founded on middle-class cowardice, which consists in always surrendering before the threat of violence, cannot fail to engender the idea that the middle class is condemned to death.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Chapter 1, 'Class War and Violence'
suggested_refs: The Action française circle of Charles Maurras, 1909-1910

stops.name: Paris, the article on Péguy's Joan of Arc
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia to the day: an article by Sorel on Charles Péguy's treatment of Joan of Arc appears in the newspaper Action française on 14 April 1910.
stops.campa: On the fourteenth of April the paper Action française prints Sorel on Charles Péguy's Joan of Arc. Péguy has just published his mystery of the girl from Domrémy, a socialist's saint rebuilt as France's own, and Sorel takes it up in a royalist paper. It is the exact case his theory describes: a figure held whole in the mind of a people, doing its work now, five centuries after the fire at Rouen, without needing to be true in the way a report is true.
suggested_refs: Charles Péguy, Le Mystère de la charité de Jeanne d'Arc (1910)
Georges Sorel, article in Action française, 14 April 1910

stops.name: Paris, La Cité française that never appears
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia's article on the Cercle Proudhon that Sorel brought Georges Valois and Édouard Berth together to plan La Cité française, a short-lived project; the month is an ordering inference.
stops.campa: Sorel puts Georges Valois and Édouard Berth in the same room to plan a review, La Cité française, meant to hold nationalists and syndicalists inside a single argument against the liberal Republic. Valois comes from Maurras, Berth from the unions, and the thing they are attempting has no name yet in any language. The room does not come to nothing: nearly everything that happens in Paris on this frontier over the next two years happens among these four or five men. The review comes to a prospectus, some letters, a title.
stops.quote: The expression 'class war,' for example, is employed in the most improper manner.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Chapter 1, 'Class War and Violence'
suggested_refs: The stillborn review La Cité française, planned 1910

stops.name: Paris, the Cercle Proudhon founded without him
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Cercle Proudhon first met on 17 November 1911 and was founded on 16 December 1911, per French Wikipedia. That article also records Sorel as hostile to the Circle from the start, fearing it would make young men less able to understand Proudhon. Historians dispute how sincere and how sustained that hostility was, and a gathering pass wrongly reported it as a later disavowal; the dispute is not resolved here.
stops.campa: Young monarchists and syndicalists found the Cercle Proudhon in Paris, taking their name from the printer's son who wanted neither the state nor capital, and taking most of their arguments from Sorel. He is hostile to it from the start. His stated fear is that the Circle will leave its young men less able to understand Proudhon, not more, and he says so before it has met twice. How sincere that hostility was, and how long he held it, is a thing the historians of the French right have never settled. The Circle goes on quoting him either way.
stops.quote: It is the myth in its entirety which is alone important: its parts are only of interest in so far as they bring out the main idea.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Chapter 4, 'The Proletarian Strike'
suggested_refs: Cahiers du Cercle Proudhon, Paris, 1912-1914

stops.name: Paris, L'Indépendance, and out again
stops.date_confidence: attested by English and French Wikipedia that Sorel wrote for L'Indépendance alongside Édouard Berth and Georges Valois, across a range given as 1911-1913, and that he left over the review's nationalist tone. The date falls inside that window to order the segment and asserts nothing; the sources do not fix when within 1911-1913 he left, nor whether that came before or after the Cercle Proudhon's founding.
stops.campa: He writes for L'Indépendance with Berth and Valois, and then he leaves it, because the nationalism has begun to run the review instead of the other way round. The man the right is busy claiming walks out of the right's paper. He is sixty-four years old, living on an engineer's pension in a suburb, with no organisation behind him and no income from any of this writing. Asked whether the years since 1906 have shown him anything that spoils the argument of his book, he answers in print.
stops.quote: I have often been asked lately if I have not observed any facts since 1906 which invalidated some of the arguments set forth in this book. On the contrary, I am more than ever convinced of the value of this philosophy of violence.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), 'A Note to the Third French Edition'
suggested_refs: L'Indépendance, Paris, 1911-1913

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, against the Union sacrée
stops.date_confidence: attested by English Wikipedia that Sorel publicly opposed the Union sacrée, the wartime political truce declared at the outbreak of the First World War; the month is that of the declaration itself and the exact date of his statement is not recorded in the consulted sources.
stops.campa: France declares the Union sacrée, and every party including the socialists agrees to stop fighting each other for the duration of the war. Sorel opposes it publicly, from the house at Boulogne. He has spent ten years arguing that a class which stops fighting stops existing as a class, and here is the whole of French socialism agreeing to exactly that inside a single week, in the name of the nation. He is sixty-six. He has no paper of his own, no party to be expelled from, and the militants he wrote for are in uniform by September. The truce holds four years.
suggested_refs: The Union sacrée of August 1914

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, the greatest theorist since Marx
stops.date_confidence: attested by French Wikipedia that Sorel praised the Russian Revolution and called Lenin the greatest theorist socialism has had since Marx; the month is that of the October Revolution by the Gregorian calendar and the date of the remark itself is not fixed in the consulted sources.
stops.campa: The Bolsheviks take power in Petrograd, and the old engineer, seventy years old and never once a member of anything, declares for them. He calls Lenin the greatest theorist socialism has had since Karl Marx. What he sees is not a programme executed on schedule but a myth acted on: men who refused to wait for the conditions to ripen, in the most backward country in Europe, against every prediction the orthodox had made. He will never go to Russia and never meet a Bolshevik. Lenin, for his part, had read him and thought him a muddler.
suggested_refs: Lenin's dismissal of Sorel as a muddler, reported in Italian Wikipedia, 'Georges Sorel'

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, writing for the Bolsheviks in Italian
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date; English and French Wikipedia attest that after 1917 Sorel wrote for a Soviet-aligned publication and for Italian newspapers defending the Bolsheviks, with no year given. A gathering pass added that he remained hostile to Gabriele D'Annunzio and to the rising fascist movement; that clause is contradicted by the same sources and is not carried here.
stops.campa: In his last years he writes in defence of the Bolsheviks, in a Soviet-aligned publication and in the Italian press, which has always printed him faster than the French. Italy is in its two red years and then in its black ones. Gabriele D'Annunzio has taken Fiume with a column of volunteers, and the syndicalists Sorel corresponded with are drafting programmes for men in black shirts. What he made of all this is contested: one line of report has him hostile to it, another approving, and both lines are drawn from him. He is seventy-two and still reading everything.
stops.quote: To examine the effects of violence it is necessary to start from its distant consequences and not from its immediate results.
stops.quote_source: Georges Sorel, Reflections on Violence, trans. T. E. Hulme (1915), Introduction to the First Publication
suggested_refs: Sorel's postwar articles in the Italian press

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, Matériaux d'une théorie du prolétariat
stops.date_confidence: the year of publication is attested by French Wikipedia; the month is an ordering inference.
stops.campa: He publishes Matériaux d'une théorie du prolétariat, a collection rather than a system: materials, in the title's own word, for a theory he never finishes and never intends to close. Thirty years of writing and not one book that lays out a doctrine from first principles. The habit is deliberate: a theory of the proletariat that arrived complete would be the thing he spent his life saying could not exist, since the class has to make itself. Whether he ever meant to write the theory the materials were for, no note of his says.
suggested_refs: Matériaux d'une théorie du prolétariat (Paris, 1919)

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, the sentence about Mussolini
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction as to date and contested as to substance. English Wikipedia records Sorel describing Mussolini approvingly as a leader of a consecrated battalion saluting the flags of Italy with his sword; no date is given for the remark, and the extent of his approval, set against his simultaneous praise of Lenin, is disputed by historians. The date orders the segment only.
stops.campa: Somewhere in his last years he says of Benito Mussolini that he is a leader of a consecrated battalion, saluting the flags of Italy with his sword. He says in the same period that Lenin is the greatest theorist since Marx. Both sentences are his. He dies in August 1922, two months before the March on Rome, having never seen what the second man does with the state, and the argument about what he would have said has run for a century without a witness.
suggested_refs: Zeev Sternhell, Ni droite ni gauche (1983), the modern reopening of the question

stops.name: Boulogne-sur-Seine, death in the house
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by English and French Wikipedia: he dies at Boulogne-sur-Seine, aged 74, in the town where he had lived since 1892.
stops.campa: Georges Sorel dies on the twenty-ninth of August, seventy-four years old, in the house at Boulogne he moved into thirty years before with a woman he was not allowed to marry. He leaves no party, no school, no chair, no journal and no fortune. He leaves one book, by then read in French, Italian and English, and a quarrel over what it meant. The quarrel begins almost at once and is conducted from this point onward entirely by other people. He is buried a few days later, neither at Boulogne nor at Cherbourg.
suggested_refs: Death record, Boulogne-sur-Seine, 29 August 1922

stops.name: Tenay, the vault of Jean-Baptiste David
stops.date_confidence: the burial at Tenay in the Ain is attested by French Wikipedia, which says he is buried in the vault of his adoptive son Jean-Baptiste David and rests opposite his companion. Only the year is attested; the month is an ordering default. Two gathering passes reversed the parentage, making Jean-Baptiste Marie David's son rather than Sorel's, and three gave three different coordinates for Tenay; the commune point of 45.9186/5.5106 is used.
stops.campa: He is carried east to Tenay, a small commune of the Ain in the folds of the Bugey, and laid in the vault of his adoptive son Jean-Baptiste David, opposite Marie David, twenty-five years dead. It is a family grave in a village that has nothing else to do with him, four hundred kilometres from the table where he wrote and six hundred from the port where he was born. France will in time put his name on streets in Boulogne-Billancourt, in Perpignan, in Cherbourg, and on one street in Le Port on Réunion. The grave itself is left to the household.
suggested_refs: The cemetery of Tenay, Ain; the David family vault
Streets named for Sorel at Boulogne-Billancourt, Perpignan, Cherbourg-en-Cotentin, Le Port (Réunion) and Saint-Cyprien, undated in the sources

stops.name: Tenay, the monument the family refuses
stops.date_confidence: attested by Italian Wikipedia, which reports that in October 1932 the fascist regime, informed of the state of abandonment of Sorel's tomb, offered to take charge of it and raise a monument, and that the family refused. A gathering pass attributed the offer specifically to the Italian ambassador to France acting for Mussolini; the source names the regime, not an ambassador. The day is not recorded.
stops.campa: Ten years after the burial, word reaches Rome that the grave at Tenay is neglected. The regime offers to take charge of the tomb and raise a monument on it, an Italian state proposing to build in a French village cemetery for a French writer who never joined anything. The family answers that the condition of the grave concerns only the family and no one else. The offer and the refusal both fall inside October 1932, and the stone stays as it is. No monument is built.
stops.quote: concerned only the family and no one else
stops.quote_source: The Sorel family's reply to the Italian offer, October 1932, reported in Italian Wikipedia, 'Georges Sorel'
suggested_refs: Zeev Sternhell, Ni droite ni gauche (1983)
Jeremy Jennings, ed., Reflections on Violence (Cambridge, 1999)
